quote: MN 137 tells practitioners to use unification to relinquish diversity, then non-identification to relinquish unity. In MN 121, at every depth of unification the meditator audits the remaining disturbance and finds “just this much – that which depends on oneness.” Unity itself is the last stress.
hard: "relinquish diversity", "non-identification" and "audits the remaining disturbance" are abstract and unexplained, "unification", "unity" and "oneness" look like three different things, and two sutta claims plus his conclusion are crammed together with no step showing why unity is "the last stress".
plain: MN 137 gives a two-step recipe. First you use unification (gathering the mind into one) to let go of diversity (the mind spread across lots of different things). Then you use non-identification (not taking anything to be “me”) to let go of unity too. In MN 121, at every depth of unification, the meditator checks what disturbance is still left, and what they find is “just this much – that which depends on oneness.” Put together, that says unity itself is the last stress.
heading: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness

quote: To carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion. That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.
hard: Dōgen's line comes with no gloss (what "myriad things" are, what it means for things to "experience themselves", how that differs from you "experiencing" them), and the next line, "Other translations give opposite readings", leaves the reader unsure what the line even says.
plain: Dōgen sets two directions against each other. In one, you carry yourself forward and experience the myriad things (all the countless things that appear), and he calls that delusion. In the other, the myriad things come forth and experience themselves, and he calls that awakening. His words: “To carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion. That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.” Other translations give opposite readings of this line, but this one was key for me.
heading: The Myriad Things Experience Themselves
note: it is Dōgen's line, quoted; the next line says other translations differ

quote: It was a full unweaving because unified consciousness and the functioning body-world were gone, but its scope was no longer limited to sensations inside the body as with the fingers nibbāna event.

heading: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya

quote: Because we don’t now “exist” as the natural laws themselves, but rather as a fabricated abstraction from them, pain, unsatisfactoriness, and injustice still hurt and still call for a response. But once we can experientially touch ultimate reality and realize the path out of the illusory cycle, those problems don’t hold the same ultimate psychological power over us.

plain: Everything is happening according to natural laws, but we don’t live as those laws themselves. We live as a made-up abstraction built out of them, the unified sense of self. Because that’s what we are right now, pain, unsatisfactoriness, and injustice still hurt and still call for a response. But once you can touch ultimate reality (that already-perfect nature) for yourself, and see the path out of the illusory cycle of birth, death, joy, and suffering called saṃsāra, those problems stop having the same ultimate psychological power over you.
heading: What “Already Perfect” Means

quote: Every time someone claims to experience pure awareness (sat chit ananda – being, consciousness, bliss), they can still describe how it feels. So that non-duality is false.

plain: Every time someone claims to experience pure awareness (sat chit ananda: being, consciousness, bliss), they can still tell you what it feels like. But if it can be described as something felt, then there’s still a feeler and a felt, so it isn’t really one undivided thing. That’s why I say that kind of non-duality is false.
heading: Free Will Vs Conditions

Normally that fastening makes them into one settled consciousness, one self, one world, and the kind of existence that gets renewed in another birth. In the room it looked like everything was being unwoven. And since the suttas keep talking in tangles, knots, and nets, I don’t think that weaving picture is an accident.

Each of those is still bound up inside itself, so it isn’t nibbāna (nibbāna means unbinding), but it hints at it. Ud 5.10 has something similar: monastics split into a thousand bodies to clean rooms faster, until someone touches one of them and they merge back into one.

So there’s no more rebirth ahead, yet the constructed functioning that can feel pleasure and pain is still running. That’s why, in this article, “saṃsāric” means that constructed functioning itself, the part that’s capable of dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness), and not only the craving that produces another birth.

heading: Ignorance is the root

It's nibbāna when that setting-up comes completely undone (what I call unweaving).

quote: Across AN 3.47, where saṅkhata things arise, disappear, and decay while remaining; SN 22.79, on the manufacturing of experience; and the decay and assembly metaphors in DN 16 and SN 5.10, saṅkhata means “compounded,” “assembled,” or “fabricated,” not abstractly “conditioned.”

quote: Light is energy in the electromagnetic field spectrum, and energy can’t be created or destroyed. Individual photons are emitted and absorbed, but a photon has no parts to decay or disassemble. So light isn’t fabricated, even if a factory made your light bulbs.

Individual photons do get emitted and absorbed, but a photon isn't made of smaller parts, so it has nothing that could fall apart or be taken apart. So light isn't fabricated (put together from parts), even if a factory made your light bulbs.
heading: If nibbāna is “unfabricated,” is light also?

quote: Physics shows the same shape: permanence is a pattern made from nature’s impermanence, reminiscent of a mind arising as one thing and ceasing as another, and of flows tangling, getting heavy, and releasing.
hard: "the same shape" has no referent; "permanence is a pattern made from impermanence" is abstract with no example; "flows tangling, getting heavy, and releasing" calls back to ideas this part never mentions.
plain: Physics has the same pattern: things that look permanent are patterns built out of nature's constant change, like a mind that arises as one thing and ceases as another. It also fits the picture of flows tangling together, getting heavy (binding is literally heavy, as I said earlier in the essay), and then releasing.
heading: Come and See for Yourself!
